claim: WNT proteins are secreted symmetry breaking signals that interact with cell surface receptors of the FZD family to regulate a multitude of developmental processes.
source: WNT proteins are secreted symmetry breaking signals that interact with cell surface receptors of the FZD family to regulate a multitude of developmental processes.
evidence: This is a general statement about WNT proteins supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Studying selectivity between WNTs and FZDs has been hampered by the paucity of purified WNT proteins and by their apparent non-selective interactions with the FZD receptors.
source: Studying selectivity between WNTs and FZDs has been hampered by the paucity of purified WNT proteins and by their apparent non-selective interactions with the FZD receptors.
evidence: This statement reflects established challenges in the field based on prior research experience.

claim: F7L6 is an engineered protein comprised of antibody-derived single-chain variable fragments that selectively binds to human FZD7 and the co-receptor LRP6.
source: Here, we describe an engineered protein, called F7L6, comprised of antibody-derived single-chain variable fragments, that selectively binds to human FZD7 and the co-receptor LRP6.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the design and binding specificity of F7L6 as demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: F7L6 potently activates WNT/β-catenin signaling in a manner similar to Wnt3a.
source: F7L6 potently activates WNT/β-catenin signaling in a manner similar to Wnt3a.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from STF reporter assays and other signaling assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: F7L6 engages only FZD7 and none of the other FZD proteins.
source: In contrast to Wnt3a, F7L6 engages only FZD7 and none of the other FZD proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing F7L6 specificity for FZD7 through binding assays and flow cytometry.

claim: Treatment of human pluripotent stem (hPS) cells with F7L6 initiates transcriptional programs similar to those observed during primitive streak formation and subsequent gastrulation in the mammalian embryo.
source: Treatment of human pluripotent stem (hPS) cells with F7L6 initiates transcriptional programs similar to those observed during primitive streak formation and subsequent gastrulation in the mammalian embryo.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing gene expression changes in hPS cells treated with F7L6.

claim: Selective engagement and activation of FZD7 signaling is sufficient to promote mesendodermal differentiation of hPS cells.
source: This demonstrates that selective engagement and activation of FZD7 signaling is sufficient to promote mesendodermal differentiation of hPS cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from differentiation assays and gene expression analysis.

claim: The human genome encodes 19 WNTs and an equally large number of WNT receptors (Frizzled [FZD]1–10, LRP5 and 6, ROR1 and 2, RYK, PTK7 and more).
source: With the human genome encoding 19 WNTs and an equally large number of WNT receptors (Frizzled [FZD]1–10, LRP5 and 6, ROR1 and 2, RYK, PTK7 and more; reviewed in Niehrs, 2012), relatively little is known about signaling specificities between WNT ligands and their receptors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article (Niehrs, 2012) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Relatively little is known about signaling specificities between WNT ligands and their receptors.
source: With the human genome encoding 19 WNTs and an equally large number of WNT receptors (Frizzled [FZD]1–10, LRP5 and 6, ROR1 and 2, RYK, PTK7 and more; reviewed in Niehrs, 2012), relatively little is known about signaling specificities between WNT ligands and their receptors.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as of the manuscript's writing.

claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells reside in the naive state.
source: Experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells, which reside in the naive state (reviewed in Smith, 2017), have indicated a role for WNT/β-catenin signaling in self renewal and maintenance of pluripotency (Hao et al., 2006; Ogawa et al., 2006; Sato et al., 2004; ten Berge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review (Smith, 2017) and represents established knowledge.

claim: WNT/β-catenin signaling plays a role in self renewal and maintenance of pluripotency in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells, which reside in the naive state (reviewed in Smith, 2017), have indicated a role for WNT/β-catenin signaling in self renewal and maintenance of pluripotency (Hao et al., 2006; Ogawa et al., 2006; Sato et al., 2004; ten Berge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: hPS cells reside in the primed state and resemble epiblast-derived stem cells.
source: In contrast, in hPS cells, which reside in the primed state and resemble epiblast-derived stem cells (Tesar et al., 2007), WNT/β-catenin signaling drives mesendodermal lineage specification (Davidson et al., 2012; Sumi et al., 2008; Tsakiridis et al., 2014), and an analysis of transcriptome-wide gene expression changes over a time-series treatment of hPS cells with Wnt3a reveals a transcriptional response reminiscent of primitive streak formation and ensuing gastrulation (Huggins et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Tesar et al., 2007) and represents established knowledge.

claim: WNT/β-catenin signaling drives mesendodermal lineage specification in hPS cells.
source: In contrast, in hPS cells, which reside in the primed state and resemble epiblast-derived stem cells (Tesar et al., 2007), WNT/β-catenin signaling drives mesendodermal lineage specification (Davidson et al., 2012; Sumi et al., 2008; Tsakiridis et al., 2014), and an analysis of transcriptome-wide gene expression changes over a time-series treatment of hPS cells with Wnt3a reveals a transcriptional response reminiscent of primitive streak formation and ensuing gastrulation (Huggins et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: Time-series treatment of hPS cells with Wnt3a reveals a transcriptional response reminiscent of primitive streak formation and ensuing gastrulation.
source: In contrast, in hPS cells, which reside in the primed state and resemble epiblast-derived stem cells (Tesar et al., 2007), WNT/β-catenin signaling drives mesendodermal lineage specification (Davidson et al., 2012; Sumi et al., 2008; Tsakiridis et al., 2014), and an analysis of transcriptome-wide gene expression changes over a time-series treatment of hPS cells with Wnt3a reveals a transcriptional response reminiscent of primitive streak formation and ensuing gastrulation (Huggins et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Huggins et al., 2017).

claim: Short-term activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling via addition of Wnt3a promotes differentiation toward definitive endoderm (DE).
source: This is consistent with observations that short-term activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, via addition of Wnt3a, promotes differentiation toward definitive endoderm (DE) (D'Amour et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (D'Amour et al., 2006).

claim: A low level of endogenous WNT activity is detectable in undifferentiated hPS cells.
source: Furthermore, a low level of endogenous WNT activity is detectable in undifferentiated hPS cells (Blauwkamp et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2013) and is required for reprogramming of human fibroblasts to an induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell state (Ross et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Blauwkamp et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2013).

claim: Endogenous WNT activity is required for reprogramming of human fibroblasts to an induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell state.
source: Furthermore, a low level of endogenous WNT activity is detectable in undifferentiated hPS cells (Blauwkamp et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2013) and is required for reprogramming of human fibroblasts to an induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell state (Ross et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Ross et al., 2014).

claim: FZD7 plays a prominent role in the regulation of pluripotency of hPS cells.
source: The WNT receptor FZD7 plays a prominent role in the regulation of pluripotency of hPS cells (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008), and its downregulation accompanies differentiation and exit from the pluripotent stem cell state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).

claim: Downregulation of FZD7 accompanies differentiation and exit from the pluripotent stem cell state.
source: The WNT receptor FZD7 plays a prominent role in the regulation of pluripotency of hPS cells (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008), and its downregulation accompanies differentiation and exit from the pluripotent stem cell state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).

claim: hPS cells express several WNT receptors, including FZD2, 3, and 5.
source: However, since hPS cells express several WNT receptors, including FZD2, 3, and 5 (Fernandez et al., 2014; Huggins et al., 2017), it is unclear whether Wnt3a promotes mesendodermal differentiation through FZD7 or whether other FZDs are required.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Huggins et al., 2017).

claim: F7-Ab is a chimeric human/mouse IgG1 antibody derived from a bacterially produced antigen binding fragment (Fab).
source: We generated a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) to FZD7 by repurposing the variable region of our FZD7-targeting antibody (F7-Ab), a chimeric human/mouse IgG1. This antibody was derived from a bacterially produced antigen binding fragment (Fab) described in a previous study (Fernandez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Fernandez et al., 2014) and describes the experimental design.

claim: F7L6 was engineered by conjugating the FZD7-scFv and LRP6-scFv to a human IgG1 Fc.
source: We then engineered F7L6 by conjugating the FZD7-scFv and LRP6-scFv to a human IgG1 Fc to create the FZD7-specific Wnt mimetic F7L6 (complete amino acid sequence is provided in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and construction of F7L6, with reference to a figure showing the sequence.

claim: F7-Ab, F7, L6, and F7L6 are secreted from CHO cells.
source: We confirmed secretion of F7-Ab, F7, L6, and F7L6 from CHO cells by SDS-PAGE and Coomassie Blue staining and immunoblotting (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: FZD7-specific binders (F7 and F7L6) only react with lysates upon FZD7 overexpression.
source: FZD7-specific binders (F7 and F7L6) only reacted with lysates upon FZD7 overexpression (note that endogenous FZD7 expression in LRP6 KO is below the level of detection), whereas LRP6-specific binders (L6 and F7L6) only reacted with lysates of cells expressing LRP6 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using dot blot assays.

claim: LRP6-specific binders (L6 and F7L6) only react with lysates of cells expressing LRP6.
source: FZD7-specific binders (F7 and F7L6) only reacted with lysates upon FZD7 overexpression (note that endogenous FZD7 expression in LRP6 KO is below the level of detection), whereas LRP6-specific binders (L6 and F7L6) only reacted with lysates of cells expressing LRP6 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using dot blot assays.

claim: F7-Ab binds to the 'neck' region between the cysteine-rich domain (CRD) and the first transmembrane domain of FZD7.
source: To further characterize the specificity of F7-Ab, we mapped its binding site to the 'neck' region between the cysteine-rich domain (CRD) and the first transmembrane domain of FZD7 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from epitope mapping experiments shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: F7-Ab only reacts with human FZD7 (hFZD7) and not with mouse Fzd7 (mFzd7).
source: Despite the high degree of homology between human and mouse Fzd7 (hFZD7 and mFzd7, respectively), F7-Ab only reacts with hFZD7 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A single amino acid change at position 188 from leucine to proline (P188) renders hFZD7 non-reactive to F7-Ab.
source: A single amino acid change at position 188 from leucine to proline (P188) renders hFZD7 non-reactive to F7-Ab, whereas the corresponding amino acid change in mFzd7 (L188) restores F7-Ab reactivity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E using mutant constructs.

claim: The F7-Ab epitope maps to an eight amino acid stretch containing L188.
source: Using fusion proteins between glutathione S-transferase (GST) and the FZD7 neck region followed by sequential shortening of the neck region, we mapped the F7-Ab epitope to an eight amino acid stretch containing L188 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F using GST fusion proteins.

claim: F7-Ab does not cross-react with the other nine human FZD receptors (FZD1-6, 8–10).
source: Since FZD proteins are highly conserved and several available FZD antibodies react with multiple FZD proteins (for example, OMP-18R5/Vantictumab reacts with FZD1, 2, 5, 7, and 8), we confirmed that F7-Ab does not cross-react with the other nine human FZD receptors (FZD1-6, 8–10) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G using flow cytometry.

claim: All FZD proteins (FZD1-10) are expressed on the cell surface.
source: To rule out the possibility that some FZDs fail to react with F7-Ab because they do not reach the cell surface, we performed confocal microscopy. This analysis confirmed that all FZD proteins were expressed on the cell surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 using confocal microscopy.

claim: F7-Ab, F7, and F7L6 are specific to hFZD7 and do not cross-react with any of the other nine human FZD proteins or with mFzd7.
source: Taken together, F7-Ab, and hence F7 and F7L6, are specific to hFZD7 and do not cross-react with any of the other nine human FZD proteins or with mFzd7.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: F7L6 activates WNT/β-catenin signaling by heterodimerizing FZD7 and LRP6.
source: The bispecific binder, F7L6, activates WNT/β-catenin signaling by heterodimerizing FZD7 and LRP6 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 2A.

claim: F7L6 activates the Super TOP-Flash (STF) WNT reporter in HEK293T cells.
source: We confirmed F7L6 signaling activity using HEK293T cells stably transfected with the WNT reporter Super TOP-Flash (STF) (Veeman et al., 2003; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B using luciferase reporter assays.

claim: Single binders to FZD7 (F7) or LRP6 (L6) do not activate WNT signaling.
source: As expected, single binders to FZD7 (F7) or LRP6 (L6) did not activate signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Activity of F7L6 is potently augmented by addition of R-Spondin1 (RSPO1).
source: As is the case with native WNT proteins, activity of F7L6 is potently augmented by addition of R-Spondin1 (RSPO1) (Kim et al., 2008; Figure 2C) with potency in the single-digit nanomolar range.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to prior work (Kim et al., 2008).

claim: Addition of RSPO1 increased F7L6 activity approximately 10-fold.
source: Interestingly, addition of RSPO1 increased F7L6 activity approximately 10-fold, but only augmented the activities of Wnt3a or FLAg FP+P-L1+3, a previously published WNT mimetic (Tao et al., 2019), by twofold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of RSPO1 augmented the activities of Wnt3a or FLAg FP+P-L1+3 by twofold.
source: Interestingly, addition of RSPO1 increased F7L6 activity approximately 10-fold, but only augmented the activities of Wnt3a or FLAg FP+P-L1+3, a previously published WNT mimetic (Tao et al., 2019), by twofold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: F7L6 is selective for FZD7, whereas Wnt3a and FLAg FP+P-L1+3 are capable of interacting with multiple FZDs.
source: A possible reason for this distinction is that F7L6 is selective for FZD7, whereas Wnt3a and FLAg FP+P-L1+3 are capable of interacting with multiple FZDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in RSPO1 augmentation and known properties of the molecules.

claim: F7L6 and FLAg FP+P-L1+3 retain significant activity at sub-nanomolar concentrations, whereas Wnt3a's activity is undetectable at such concentrations.
source: Furthermore, both Wnt mimetics retain significant activity at sub-nanomolar concentrations, whereas Wnt3a's activity is undetectable at such concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dose-response curves shown in the figures.

claim: F7L6 activates signaling independently of the WNT-binding cysteine-rich domain (CRD) of FZD7.
source: Interestingly, FZD7 lacking the CRD (CRD-less FZD7) activates signaling when heterodimerized to LRP6 with F7L6 while Wnt3a does not (Figure 2D), indicating that the CRD is dispensable for signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D using CRD-deleted FZD7 constructs.

claim: The CRD of FZD7 is dispensable for WNT signaling when FZD7 is heterodimerized with LRP6 by F7L6.
source: Interestingly, FZD7 lacking the CRD (CRD-less FZD7) activates signaling when heterodimerized to LRP6 with F7L6 while Wnt3a does not (Figure 2D), indicating that the CRD is dispensable for signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Appending the F7-Ab epitope of eight amino acids onto FZD2 is sufficient for F7L6 to activate WNT/β-catenin signaling through FZD2.
source: Furthermore, appending the F7-Ab epitope of eight amino acids (see Figure 1F) onto another FZD, FZD2, is sufficient for F7L6 to activate WNT/β-catenin signaling through FZD2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E using FZD2 with the appended epitope.

claim: Heterodimerization of FZD7 or FZD2 with LRP6 is sufficient for WNT pathway activation.
source: These data establish that heterodimerization of FZD7 or FZD2 with LRP6 is sufficient for pathway activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Treatment of mouse L-cells with Wnt3a activates downstream signaling, as assayed by cytoplasmic β-catenin stabilization.
source: Treatment of mouse L-cells with Wnt3a activates downstream signaling, as assayed by cytoplasmic β-catenin stabilization (Shibamoto et al., 1998), whereas treatment with F7L6 does not (Figure 2F), consistent with the lack of reactivity of F7-Ab with mouse Fzd7 (see Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and a citation to prior work (Shibamoto et al., 1998).

claim: Treatment of mouse L-cells with F7L6 does not activate downstream signaling.
source: Treatment of mouse L-cells with Wnt3a activates downstream signaling, as assayed by cytoplasmic β-catenin stabilization (Shibamoto et al., 1998), whereas treatment with F7L6 does not (Figure 2F), consistent with the lack of reactivity of F7-Ab with mouse Fzd7 (see Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Overexpression of human FZD7 in mouse L-cells is sufficient to activate signaling by F7L6.
source: However, overexpression of human FZD7 in these cells is sufficient to activate signaling by F7L6 (Figure 2F), thus confirming F7L6 signaling specificity through FZD7.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The kinetics of β-catenin stabilization in L-cells is similar for Wnt3a and F7L6, being first detectable between 15 and 30 min after stimulation.
source: The kinetics of β-catenin stabilization in L-cells is similar for Wnt3a and F7L6, being first detectable between 15 and 30 min after stimulation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G using time-course immunoblotting.

claim: F7L6 activates expression of the WNT target gene SP5 in hPS cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Lastly, using reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), we demonstrated that F7L6, like Wnt3a, activates expression of the WNT target gene, SP5, in hPS cells, which express FZD7 (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008), in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: F7L6 is a bispecific bivalent (or tetravalent) molecule, potentially capable of simultaneously engaging two FZD7 and two LRP6 molecules.
source: F7L6 is a bispecific bivalent (or tetravalent) molecule, potentially capable of simultaneously engaging two FZD7 and two LRP6 molecules, thus leading to receptor oligomerization, which has been proposed to promote intracellular signalosome formation (DeBruine et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the molecular design of F7L6 and a citation to prior work on receptor oligomerization (DeBruine et al., 2017).

claim: Receptor oligomerization has been proposed to promote intracellular signalosome formation.
source: F7L6 is a bispecific bivalent (or tetravalent) molecule, potentially capable of simultaneously engaging two FZD7 and two LRP6 molecules, thus leading to receptor oligomerization, which has been proposed to promote intracellular signalosome formation (DeBruine et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (DeBruine et al., 2017).

claim: F7L6-sc is a single-chain version of F7L6 that is predicted to engage one FZD7 and one LRP6 receptor.
source: To address whether FZD7-LRP6 heterodimerization alone is sufficient for signaling, we deleted the Fc portion to generate a single-chain F7L6 (F7L6-sc) that is predicted to engage one FZD7 and one LRP6 receptor.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of F7L6-sc.

claim: F7L6-sc activated Wnt signaling, albeit to a lesser extent than the tetravalent F7L6 protein.
source: F7L6-sc activated Wnt signaling, albeit to a lesser extent than the tetravalent F7L6 protein (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The maximal response in the STF assay for F7L6 was approximately twice that for F7L6-sc.
source: Interestingly, the maximal response in the STF assay for F7L6 was approximately twice that for F7L6-sc.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: F7L6-sc is monomeric in solution and does not form larger oligomers.
source: Size exclusion chromatography confirmed that F7L6-sc is monomeric in solution and does not form larger oligomers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 using size exclusion chromatography.

claim: A 1:1 association of FZD7 and LRP6 is sufficient to activate downstream WNT signaling.
source: These data demonstrate that a 1:1 association of FZD7 and LRP6 is sufficient to activate downstream signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from F7L6-sc experiments.

claim: Modulating WNT/β-catenin signaling is crucial for differentiation of hPS cells into mesendoderm and definitive endoderm (DE).
source: Previous studies have shown that modulating WNT/β-catenin signaling is crucial for differentiation of hPS cells into mesendoderm and DE (D'Amour et al., 2006; Huggins et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2013; Martyn et al., 2018; Yoney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Wnt3a and GSK3-inhibitors are frequently used interchangeably as WNT pathway activators in differentiation protocols.
source: Wnt3a and GSK3-inhibitors (e.g. CHIR99021, CHIR98014, BIO, Li) (Klein and Melton, 1996; Ring et al., 2003; Sato et al., 2004; Stambolic et al., 1996) are frequently used interchangeably as WNT pathway activators in these differentiation protocols (Gertow et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2015; Loh et al., 2014; Naujok et al., 2014; Teo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: FZD7 transduces the Wnt3a signal.
source: We hypothesized that FZD7 mediates this process, because it transduces the Wnt3a signal (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017) and regulates the pluripotent state (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017).

claim: FZD7 regulates the pluripotent state of hPS cells.
source: We hypothesized that FZD7 mediates this process, because it transduces the Wnt3a signal (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017) and regulates the pluripotent state (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).

claim: F7L6, Wnt3a, and CHIR98014 treatment significantly altered expression of 525, 708, and 1646 genes, respectively.
source: F7L6, Wnt3, and CHIR treatment significantly altered expression of 525, 708, and 1646 genes, respectively (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4 and supplementary files.

claim: A majority of genes (428 of 805 genes) in the F7L6 and Wnt3a lists overlapped.
source: A majority of genes (428 of 805 genes) (Supplementary file 1E and F) in the F7L6 and Wnt3a lists overlapped, whereas expression changes of a large number of genes was unique to CHIR (1009 genes) (Supplementary file 1G), highlighting the substantial differences when the pathway is activated at the level of receptor rather than at the level of GSK3 inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in supplementary files.

claim: Expression changes of a large number of genes (1009 genes) was unique to CHIR treatment.
source: A majority of genes (428 of 805 genes) (Supplementary file 1E and F) in the F7L6 and Wnt3a lists overlapped, whereas expression changes of a large number of genes was unique to CHIR (1009 genes) (Supplementary file 1G), highlighting the substantial differences when the pathway is activated at the level of receptor rather than at the level of GSK3 inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in supplementary files.

claim: Gene expression changes in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 were overall highly similar.
source: Gene expression changes in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 were overall highly similar, with robust activation of classic markers of mesendoderm (i.e. GSC, MIXL1, SP5 and T) and DE (i.e. LEFTY1, EOMES, CER1, FOXA2, CXCR4, and SOX17) and downregulation of pluripotency markers, such as POU3F1, FZD7, and PODXL (TRA-1–81).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Wnt3a and F7L6 treatment led to robust activation of classic markers of mesendoderm (GSC, MIXL1, SP5 and T) and DE (LEFTY1, EOMES, CER1, FOXA2, CXCR4, and SOX17).
source: Gene expression changes in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 were overall highly similar, with robust activation of classic markers of mesendoderm (i.e. GSC, MIXL1, SP5 and T) and DE (i.e. LEFTY1, EOMES, CER1, FOXA2, CXCR4, and SOX17) and downregulation of pluripotency markers, such as POU3F1, FZD7, and PODXL (TRA-1–81).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Wnt3a and F7L6 treatment led to downregulation of pluripotency markers, such as POU3F1, FZD7, and PODXL (TRA-1–81).
source: Gene expression changes in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 were overall highly similar, with robust activation of classic markers of mesendoderm (i.e. GSC, MIXL1, SP5 and T) and DE (i.e. LEFTY1, EOMES, CER1, FOXA2, CXCR4, and SOX17) and downregulation of pluripotency markers, such as POU3F1, FZD7, and PODXL (TRA-1–81).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Induction of established WNT target genes (DKK1, AXIN2, WLS, WNT3, and NKD1) was more potent with Wnt3a than with F7L6.
source: However, there were some notable differences between Wnt3a and F7L6 treatments. For example, induction of established WNT target genes, such as DKK1, AXIN2, WLS, WNT3, and NKD1, was more potent with Wnt3a than with F7L6.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Induction of genes such as T, SP5, GSC, and FOXA2 was slightly delayed for F7L6 relative to Wnt3a.
source: Also, induction of genes, such as T, SP5, GSC, and FOXA2, was slightly delayed for F7L6 relative to Wnt3a.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Differences between F7L6 and Wnt3a are potentially due to F7L6 solely engaging FZD7 and LRP6, while Wnt3a promotes signaling through multiple FZD-LRP5/6 heterodimers.
source: These differences are potentially due to F7L6 solely engaging FZD7 and LRP6 to promote downstream signaling, while Wnt3a, in contrast, promotes signaling through multiple FZD-LRP5/6 heterodimers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in gene expression and known properties of F7L6 and Wnt3a.

claim: CHIR treatment produced significantly different gene expression profiles compared to Wnt3a and F7L6, both in kinetics and amplitude.
source: In contrast to Wnt3a and F7L6, CHIR treatment produced significantly different gene expression profiles, both in kinetics and amplitude (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: All three treatments (F7L6, Wnt3a, and CHIR) activated known WNT target genes (AXIN2, DKK1, LEF1, and SP5) and mesendodermal genes (T, MIXL1, GATA4, and EOMES).
source: For example, while all three treatments activated known WNT target genes (e.g. AXIN2, DKK1, LEF1, and SP5) and mesendodermal genes (e.g. T, MIXL1, GATA4, and EOMES), CHIR did so more robustly than Wnt3a or F7L6.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: CHIR activated WNT target genes and mesendodermal genes more robustly than Wnt3a or F7L6.
source: For example, while all three treatments activated known WNT target genes (e.g. AXIN2, DKK1, LEF1, and SP5) and mesendodermal genes (e.g. T, MIXL1, GATA4, and EOMES), CHIR did so more robustly than Wnt3a or F7L6.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Differences in gene activation by CHIR are likely attributable to the fact that CHIR acts downstream of the receptor complexes and hence is not restricted by receptor availability.
source: Such differences are likely attributable to the fact that CHIR acts downstream of the receptor complexes and hence is not restricted by receptor availability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of action of CHIR as a GSK3 inhibitor.

claim: CHIR failed to activate expression of certain definitive endoderm markers, in particular FOXA2 and SOX17.
source: Furthermore, while all three treatments activated expression of Wnt pathway and mesendodermal genes, CHIR failed to activate expression of certain genes, in particular the DE markers FOXA2 and SOX 17 (and to a lesser extent CER and GSC), an effect we validated using RT-qPCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and RT-qPCR validation shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of CXCR4, which encodes a cell surface receptor commonly used to enrich DE populations, was activated by CHIR.
source: Interestingly, expression of other DE markers, such as CXCR4, which encodes a cell surface receptor commonly used to enrich DE populations using flow cytometry (D'Amour et al., 2005; McGrath et al., 1999), was activated by CHIR (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and citations to prior studies.

claim: Sustained activation of WNT/β-catenin signaling by GSK3 inhibition with CHIR produces significant differences compared to selective pathway activation with either Wnt3a or F7L6.
source: These results indicate that sustained activation of WNT/β-catenin signaling by GSK3 inhibition with CHIR produces significant differences compared to selective pathway activation with either Wnt3a or F7L6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq data analysis comparing the three treatments.

claim: Both Wnt3a and F7L6 activated early WNT target genes with similar kinetics.
source: We used RT-qPCR to validate changes in expression of several genes within these clusters in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 over a 6-hr time course in hPS cells. Both Wnt3a and F7L6 activated these early target genes with similar kinetics, with expression of AXIN2, SOX9, and ARL4A at 3 hr (Figure 5C–E) and NKX1-2, NKD1 and FGF18 at 6 hr (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Heterodimerization of FZD7 and LRP6 by F7L6 is sufficient to elicit a transcriptional response in hPS cells similar to that elicited by Wnt3a.
source: These findings support that heterodimerization of FZD7 and LRP6 by F7L6 is sufficient to elicit a transcriptional response in hPS cells similar to that elicited by Wnt3a and likely does not involve the recruitment of additional receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RT-qPCR data comparing F7L6 and Wnt3a.

claim: F7L6 treatment likely does not involve the recruitment of additional receptors beyond FZD7 and LRP6.
source: These findings support that heterodimerization of FZD7 and LRP6 by F7L6 is sufficient to elicit a transcriptional response in hPS cells similar to that elicited by Wnt3a and likely does not involve the recruitment of additional receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of transcriptional responses between F7L6 and Wnt3a.

claim: F7L6 potently activated expression of both T-GFP and SOX17-eGFP reporters in hPS cells.
source: F7L6 potently activated expression of both reporters (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—videos 1 and 2), with T-GFP expression first detectable at 24 hr (Figure 6B,D) and SOX17-eGFP at 36 hr (Figure 6C,E).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: T-GFP expression was first detectable at 24 hr after F7L6 treatment.
source: F7L6 potently activated expression of both reporters (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—videos 1 and 2), with T-GFP expression first detectable at 24 hr (Figure 6B,D) and SOX17-eGFP at 36 hr (Figure 6C,E).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: SOX17-eGFP expression was first detectable at 36 hr after F7L6 treatment.
source: F7L6 potently activated expression of both reporters (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—videos 1 and 2), with T-GFP expression first detectable at 24 hr (Figure 6B,D) and SOX17-eGFP at 36 hr (Figure 6C,E).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Wnt3a activated expression of both T-GFP and SOX17-eGFP transgenes with similar temporal kinetics to F7L6, but induction was significantly lower than with F7L6.
source: Wnt3a likewise activated expression of both transgenes with similar temporal kinetics, however, their induction was significantly lower than with F7L6 (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The difference in potency between F7L6 and Wnt3a is likely due to the fact that Wnt3a is more unstable than F7L6 in culture conditions.
source: This difference in potency between F7L6 and Wnt3a is likely due to the fact that Wnt3a is more unstable than F7L6 in these culture conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of Wnt3a and F7L6.

claim: CHIR treatment yielded reporter gene expression distinct from both F7L6 and Wnt3a, with an early peak in T-GFP expression that subsequently declines.
source: Treatment with CHIR yielded reporter gene expression distinct from both F7L6 and Wnt3a, with an early peak in T-GFP expression that subsequently declines (Figure 6B,D) and no induction of the SOX17-eGFP reporter (Figure 6C,E).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: CHIR treatment resulted in no induction of the SOX17-eGFP reporter.
source: Treatment with CHIR yielded reporter gene expression distinct from both F7L6 and Wnt3a, with an early peak in T-GFP expression that subsequently declines (Figure 6B,D) and no induction of the SOX17-eGFP reporter (Figure 6C,E).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Activation of FZD7 alone is sufficient to promote definitive endoderm (DE) formation.
source: As expected, expression of the pluripotency marker OCT4 (POU5F1) declined over the 3 days of differentiation with a more potent effect by F7L6 compared to Wnt3a (Figure 7B). Concurrently, expression of endodermal markers, SOX17, CXCR4 and FOXA2, increased upon treatment with F7L6 to a similar extent as Wnt3a (Figure 7B), indicating that activation of FZD7 alone is sufficient to promote DE formation.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from DE differentiation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: F7L6 treatment led to a more potent decline in OCT4 (POU5F1) expression compared to Wnt3a during DE differentiation.
source: As expected, expression of the pluripotency marker OCT4 (POU5F1) declined over the 3 days of differentiation with a more potent effect by F7L6 compared to Wnt3a (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of endodermal markers (SOX17, CXCR4 and FOXA2) increased upon treatment with F7L6 to a similar extent as Wnt3a.
source: Concurrently, expression of endodermal markers, SOX17, CXCR4 and FOXA2, increased upon treatment with F7L6 to a similar extent as Wnt3a (Figure 7B), indicating that activation of FZD7 alone is sufficient to promote DE formation.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A specific WNT signal involving WNT9A and FZD9 increased the efficiency of hematopoietic differentiation from hPS cells.
source: We previously showed that a specific WNT signal involving WNT9A and FZD9 increased the efficiency of this differentiation protocol, as monitored by an increase in the yield of CD34/CD45 double positive cells (Grainger et al., 2019; Richter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Grainger et al., 2019; Richter et al., 2018).

claim: F7L6 treatment at days 2–4 of hematopoietic differentiation significantly reduced the number of CD34/CD45 double positive cells at day 14.
source: We found that F7L6 treatment at days 2–4 of differentiation, the treatment window we previously established to be critical for optimal differentiation, significantly reduced the number of CD34/CD45 double positive cells at day 14 relative to untreated or Wnt3a treated (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: F7L6 treatment adversely affected the percentages of CD34 and CD45 single positive cells during hematopoietic differentiation.
source: The percentages of CD34 and CD45 single positive cells were likewise adversely affected by F7L6 (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: F7L6 failed to induce expression of hematopoietic markers, including MESP1 and MIXL1 at day 4 and KDR at day 11 of differentiation.
source: RT-qPCR demonstrated that F7L6 failed to induce expression of hematopoietic markers, including MESP1 and MIXL1 at day 4 and KDR at day 11 of differentiation (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Selective activation of FZD7 with F7L6 promotes differentiation into certain lineages, such as DE, but hinders differentiation into other lineages, such as the blood lineage.
source: Therefore, selective activation of FZD7 with F7L6 promotes differentiation into certain lineages, such as DE, but hinders differentiation into other lineages, such as the blood lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differentiation experiments comparing DE and hematopoietic differentiation.

claim: Selective engagement and heterodimerization of FZD7 and LRP6 with F7L6 is sufficient to drive the differentiation program promoted by Wnt3a in hPS cells.
source: We demonstrated that selective engagement and heterodimerization of FZD7 and LRP6 with F7L6 is sufficient to drive the differentiation program promoted by Wnt3a in hPS cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FZD7 is the most abundantly expressed FZD receptor in hPS cells.
source: FZD7 is the most abundantly expressed FZD receptor in hPS cells, and its knockdown by RNA interference disrupts expression of pluripotency-associated genes, such as POU5F1/OCT4 and NANOG (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).

claim: Knockdown of FZD7 by RNA interference disrupts expression of pluripotency-associated genes, such as POU5F1/OCT4 and NANOG.
source: FZD7 is the most abundantly expressed FZD receptor in hPS cells, and its knockdown by RNA interference disrupts expression of pluripotency-associated genes, such as POU5F1/OCT4 and NANOG (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).

claim: Inhibition of endogenous WNT processing in hPS cells using PORCN inhibitors interferes with their pluripotency.
source: Likewise, inhibition of endogenous WNT processing in hPS cells using PORCN inhibitors also interferes with their pluripotency (Fernandez et al., 2014), suggesting that an endogenous WNT signal mediated by FZD7 is required to maintain hPS cells in an undifferentiated and pluripotent state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Fernandez et al., 2014).

claim: An endogenous WNT signal mediated by FZD7 is required to maintain hPS cells in an undifferentiated and pluripotent state.
source: Likewise, inhibition of endogenous WNT processing in hPS cells using PORCN inhibitors also interferes with their pluripotency (Fernandez et al., 2014), suggesting that an endogenous WNT signal mediated by FZD7 is required to maintain hPS cells in an undifferentiated and pluripotent state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study and the role of FZD7.

claim: Ectopic activation of WNT/β-catenin signaling with Wnt3a or F7L6 leads to hPS cell differentiation along the mesendodermal lineage.
source: On the other hand, ectopic activation of WNT/β-catenin signaling, either with Wnt3a or with F7L6, leads to hPS cell differentiation along the mesendodermal lineage.
evidence: This is supported by the differentiation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Wnt3a and F7L6 elicit nearly identical transcriptional responses associated with early embryonic development, including formation of the primitive streak and gastrulation movements.
source: Whole transcriptome analysis revealed that Wnt3a and F7L6 elicit nearly identical transcriptional responses associated with early embryonic development, including formation of the primitive streak and gastrulation movements.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment with a GSK3 inhibitor (CHIR98014) elicits significantly different effects compared to Wnt3a.
source: Interestingly, we found that treatment with a GSK3 inhibitor (CHIR98014), which is commonly used interchangeably with Wnt3a, elicits significantly different effects.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and differentiation data comparing CHIR to Wnt3a and F7L6.

claim: Over a 2-day treatment window, Wnt3a and F7L6 led to robust expression of the endodermal markers FOXA2 and SOX17, whereas the GSK3 inhibitor did not.
source: Most notably, we observed that over a 2-day treatment window, Wnt3a and F7L6 led to robust expression of the endodermal markers FOXA2 and SOX17, whereas the GSK3 inhibitor did not.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GSK3 inhibition elicited significantly different dynamics and kinetics of β-catenin accumulation and localization compared to Wnt3a.
source: Consistent with these observations, Kafri et al. found that GSK3 inhibition elicited significantly different dynamics and kinetics of β-catenin accumulation and localization compared to Wnt3a (Kafri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Kafri et al., 2016).

claim: Specific activation of WNT/FZD signaling is important to recapitulate developmental processes.
source: These findings indicate that specific activation of WNT/FZD signaling is important to recapitulate developmental processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed differences between receptor-level and GSK3-level pathway activation.

claim: Native WNT proteins interact promiscuously with multiple receptors.
source: First, native WNT proteins interact promiscuously with multiple receptors. For example, Wnt3a interacts with FZD1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, and 10 (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017).

claim: Wnt3a interacts with FZD1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, and 10.
source: First, native WNT proteins interact promiscuously with multiple receptors. For example, Wnt3a interacts with FZD1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, and 10 (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017).

claim: The co-receptors LRP5 and LRP6 are functionally redundant.
source: In addition, the co-receptors LRP5 and LRP6 are functionally redundant (Kelly et al., 2004), indicating that WNT proteins can interact equivalently with either one.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Kelly et al., 2004).

claim: WNT mimetics can be engineered to interact with greater selectivity for cell surface receptors compared to native WNT proteins.
source: In contrast, WNT mimetics can be engineered to interact with greater selectivity for cell surface receptors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the design and characterization of F7L6 in the manuscript.

claim: In vivo, WNT-FZD signaling specificity is regulated in part by co-receptors.
source: In vivo, WNT-FZD signaling specificity is regulated in part by co-receptors.
evidence: This is supported by examples of co-receptors like Reck, Gpr124, and Egfr cited in the manuscript.

claim: Reck and Gpr124 act together to promote Wnt7a-Fzd-Lrp5/6 signaling to promote angiogenesis in the developing central nervous system.
source: For example, Reck, a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored cell surface protein, acts together with Gpr124, a 7-transmembrane protein, to promote Wnt7a-Fzd-Lrp5/6 signaling to promote angiogenesis in the developing central nervous system (Cho et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2019; Eubelen et al., 2018; Vallon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Egfr mediates Wnt9a-Fzd9-Lrp5/6 signaling during hematopoietic development in zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, we recently identified a novel function for Egfr in mediating Wnt9a-Fzd9-Lrp5/6 signaling during hematopoietic development in zebrafish (Grainger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Grainger et al., 2019).

claim: Engineered proteins like F7L6 may overcome the need for the recruitment of specificity-conferring co-receptors.
source: The use of engineered proteins capable of engaging specific WNT receptors, such as F7L6, may overcome the need for the recruitment of specificity-conferring co-receptors, such as Reck, Gpr124 and Egfr, and thus replace the need for purification of biologically active WNT proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential advantages of WNT mimetics.

claim: Purification of native WNT proteins has proven extremely difficult, requiring 3 to 4 chromatography steps with yields of approximately 0.1 mg per liter of WNT conditioned medium.
source: Purification of native WNT proteins has proven extremely difficult, requiring 3 to 4 chromatography steps with yields of approximately 0.1 mg per liter of WNT conditioned medium (Willert, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Willert, 2008).

claim: WNT proteins are lipid modified, rendering them highly hydrophobic and necessitating the addition of detergents to maintain their solubility in aqueous conditions.
source: Furthermore, WNT proteins are lipid modified (Takada et al., 2006; Willert et al., 2003), rendering them highly hydrophobic and necessitating the addition of detergents to maintain their solubility in aqueous conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Takada et al., 2006; Willert et al., 2003).

claim: At low concentrations the activity of Wnt3a is rapidly extinguished and nearly undetectable.
source: Consistent with its poor physicochemical properties, at low concentrations the activity of Wnt3a is rapidly extinguished and nearly undetectable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dose-response curves in the manuscript.

claim: F7L6 is entirely comprised of engineered immunoglobulin sequences and hence is soluble and stable in standard biologically compatible buffers.
source: In contrast, F7L6, which is entirely comprised of engineered immunoglobulin sequences and hence is soluble and stable in standard biologically compatible buffers, retains signaling activity at significantly lower concentrations.
evidence: This is based on the molecular design of F7L6 and experimental data showing its activity.

claim: F7L6 retains signaling activity at significantly lower concentrations compared to Wnt3a.
source: In contrast, F7L6, which is entirely comprised of engineered immunoglobulin sequences and hence is soluble and stable in standard biologically compatible buffers, retains signaling activity at significantly lower concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dose-response curves in the manuscript.

claim: F7L6 can be purified using a single affinity binding step, with an approximate yield of 2.5 mg per liter of conditioned media.
source: In addition, by appending tags, such as Fc or 6x-His, F7L6 can be purified using a single affinity binding step, with an approximate yield of 2.5 mg per liter of conditioned media.
evidence: This describes the purification method and yield for F7L6.

claim: Several other groups have described recombinant proteins similar in design to F7L6 and capable of heterodimerizing FZDs and LRP5/6.
source: Several other groups have described recombinant proteins similar in design to F7L6 and capable of heterodimerizing FZDs and LRP5/6 (Chen et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2019; Janda et al., 2017; Miao et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Other WNT agonists engage the CRD of FZD, whereas the FZD7-binding arm of F7L6 binds the linker, or neck region, between the CRD and the first transmembrane domain of FZD7.
source: In contrast to these other WNT agonists that engage the CRD of FZD, the FZD7-binding arm of F7L6 binds the linker, or neck region, between the CRD and the first transmembrane domain of FZD7.
evidence: This is based on the epitope mapping data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The neck region of FZD7 is poorly conserved among the ten FZD receptors.
source: Since this neck region is poorly conserved among the ten FZD receptors, we were able to exclusively engage FZD7 and no other FZD, including mouse Fzd7.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and experimental data showing F7L6 specificity.

claim: Aside from docking a WNT protein, the CRD has no additional role in activating the downstream signaling events.
source: Therefore, aside from docking a WNT protein, the CRD has no additional role in activating the downstream signaling events.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that CRD-less FZD7 can signal when engaged by F7L6.

claim: WNTs can dimerize FZD CRDs either in a 1:2 or a 2:2 stoichiometry.
source: Structural studies have revealed that WNTs can dimerize FZD CRDs either in a 1:2 or a 2:2 stoichiometry (Hirai et al., 2019; Nile et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Higher order oligomers of WNT-FZD complexes are hypothesized to promote optimal downstream signaling.
source: These higher order oligomers are hypothesized to promote optimal downstream signaling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: A bivalent version F7L6-sc, capable of forming 1:1 FZD7-LRP6 heterodimers, promotes downstream signaling, indicating that higher order oligomerization is not strictly required for signaling.
source: Interestingly, a bivalent version, F7L6-sc, capable of forming 1:1 FZD7-LRP6 heterodimers, promotes downstream signaling, indicating that higher order oligomerization is not strictly required for signaling, consistent with previous findings by others (Miao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from F7L6-sc experiments and a citation to a prior study.

claim: Oligomerization may control signal amplitude, possibly by polymerization of the intracellular scaffolding molecules DVL and AXIN to drive signalosome formation.
source: Of note, signal saturation is approximately twofold greater for the tetravalent F7L6 version compared to the bivalent F7L6-sc version, indicating that oligomerization may control signal amplitude, possibly by polymerization of the intracellular scaffolding molecules DVL and AXIN to drive signalosome formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in signaling between F7L6 and F7L6-sc.

claim: Tetrameric ligands, such as F7L6 and those developed by others, may augment and potentiate signaling by promoting receptor clustering.
source: Therefore, tetrameric ligands, such as F7L6 and those developed by others (Chen et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2019), may augment and potentiate signaling by promoting receptor clustering.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed differences between tetravalent and bivalent versions.

claim: WNT proteins have not yet been approved for any clinical applications, owing in part to their poor physicochemical properties.
source: Despite their potent stem cell activities in vivo and their potential as therapeutics in regenerative medicine, WNT proteins have not yet been approved for any clinical applications, owing in part to their poor physicochemical properties.
evidence: This reflects the current state of WNT protein development for clinical use.

claim: Liposomal packaging has produced more stable and bioactive WNT3A, which is in early-stage clinical trials to treat patients undergoing posterolateral spinal fusion.
source: Certain formulations, such as liposomal packaging (Morrell et al., 2008), have produced more stable and bioactive WNT3A, which is in early-stage clinical trials to treat patients undergoing posterolateral spinal fusion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Morrell et al., 2008).

claim: Purification of individual WNTs has only been achieved for WNT3A and WNT5A to date.
source: However, such formulations will require purification of individual WNTs, which, to date, has only been achieved for WNT3A and WNT5A (Mikels and Nusse, 2006; Willert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Mikels and Nusse, 2006; Willert et al., 2003).

claim: WNT mimetics can be designed to target all WNT receptors and co-receptors and thus offers new opportunities for their development as therapeutics in regenerative medicine.
source: WNT mimetics, such as the one described here, can be designed to target all WNT receptors and co-receptors and thus offers new opportunities for their development as therapeutics in regenerative medicine.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of WNT mimetics.
